newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices rebound as cold spell hits Europe.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices rebound as cold spell hits Europe.

text.p: Oil prices rebounded on Tuesday, propelled by wintry weather engulfing most of northern Europe and a consequent rise in demand for heating fuel.
London futures for bellwether North Sea Brent crude rose 40 cents to $23.27 a barrel at 1645 GMT.
Storms and cold weather across northern Europe saw demand for heating oil in the key German market pick up, local oil traders said.
"Europe has come out and bought because of the snow," an oil trader in London said.
Severely depressed stocks of heating fuel in both Europe and the United States have left oil prices hostage to severe weather.
Meteorologists say Europe can expect to see an unusally early start to the winter.

A warm pocket of water in the western Atlantic Ocean, not seen for 15 years, was forcing the jet stream air flow further north than normal, sending cold air into Europe, said Jon Davis, meteorologist at brokers Smith Barney.
Dealers said expectations that weekly statistics out later on Tuesday would reveal a drawdown in U.S. heating oil stocks also helped push crude higher again.
Colder than normal weather in the U.S. last week boosted demand for heating oil.
With most OPEC producers pumping at capacity, ignoring their self-imposed quotas, there is little prospect of extra supply depressing prices enough to allow companies to rebuild stocks.

An expected freeze in OPEC's ceiling at next week's biannual conference in Vienna would keep by far the biggest slice of unused capacity -- two million barrels per day (bpd) in Saudi Arabia -- in mothballs.
Oil ministers from Nigeria, Indonesia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates have said they are in favour of keeping quotas unchanged under the 25.03 million bpd ceiling.

OPEC's Economic Commission Board (ECB) of market and technical experts from all 11 member states on Tuesday met for a second day to prepare a 1997 supply-demand outlook ahead of the ministerial conference.
